topic.subject: science
topic.title: Microorganisms: friend and foe
topic.scope: bacteria, fungi, protozoa, viruses, useful microbes, diseases, vaccines, antibiotics, food preservation, nitrogen cycle

misconceptions.statement: All microorganisms are harmful germs that cause diseases.
misconceptions.why: Media and hygiene advertisements focus almost exclusively on 'killing germs' to stay healthy.
misconceptions.fix: Most microorganisms are harmless or beneficial; they are essential for making food, medicines, and cleaning the environment.

probe.question: If we could use a magic spray to kill every single microorganism on Earth, would humans be better off?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because there would be no more diseases or infections.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see is dangerous

misconceptions.statement: Viruses are just a very small type of bacteria.
misconceptions.why: Both are microscopic and cause illness, leading students to group them into one category.
misconceptions.fix: Viruses are structurally different from bacteria and can only reproduce inside the cells of a host organism.

probe.question: Can a virus grow and multiply on its own on a piece of moist bread like bread mould does?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is a microorganism and needs food to grow.

misconceptions.root_belief: all microscopic things are the same

misconceptions.statement: Antibiotics are effective treatments for the common cold and flu.
misconceptions.why: People often take leftover antibiotics for any respiratory symptoms without understanding the cause.
misconceptions.fix: Antibiotics only kill bacteria; they have no effect on viruses, which are the cause of the common cold and flu.

probe.question: Why shouldn't a doctor prescribe penicillin for a patient with a viral flu?
probe.wrong_answer: Because penicillin is not a strong enough medicine for the flu.

misconceptions.root_belief: one medicine treats all similar illnesses

misconceptions.statement: Vaccines are a cure given to people who are already suffering from a disease.
misconceptions.why: Vaccines are often administered via injections, which students associate with being sick and visiting a clinic.
misconceptions.fix: Vaccines are preventive; they are given to healthy people to train their immune system to recognize and fight future infections.

probe.question: When is the best time to receive a polio vaccine?
probe.wrong_answer: Immediately after the person shows symptoms of the polio disease.

misconceptions.root_belief: medicine is only for the sick

misconceptions.statement: Mosquitoes and houseflies produce the diseases they carry inside their bodies.
misconceptions.why: The insect's bite or presence is the visible event that precedes the illness, so it is seen as the source.
misconceptions.fix: Insects like mosquitoes are only carriers (vectors) that transport pathogens like Plasmodium from one person to another.

probe.question: If a female Anopheles mosquito that does not carry the Plasmodium parasite bites you, will you get malaria?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the mosquito's saliva causes the malaria.

misconceptions.statement: Plants can directly absorb nitrogen gas from the atmosphere through their leaves.
misconceptions.why: Students know plants take in carbon dioxide from the air and assume they do the same for all nutrients.
misconceptions.fix: Plants cannot use atmospheric nitrogen; it must be converted into nitrates by bacteria like Rhizobium in the soil or root nodules.

probe.question: How does a leguminous plant like a pea plant get the nitrogen it needs to grow?
probe.wrong_answer: It breathes in nitrogen gas through the stomata in its leaves.

misconceptions.root_belief: organisms directly use all environmental resources
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's research on plant nutrition

misconceptions.statement: Mushrooms and other fungi are a type of plant because they grow in the ground.
misconceptions.why: Fungi are stationary and often grow in soil, leading to a classification based on superficial appearance.
misconceptions.fix: Fungi are a separate kingdom; unlike plants, they do not have chlorophyll and cannot perform photosynthesis.

probe.question: Why is a mushroom not classified as a plant by scientists?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it is a plant that just doesn't have green leaves.

misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in science

misconceptions.statement: The bacteria in curd are 'bad' germs, but we eat them anyway.
misconceptions.why: The word 'bacteria' has a strong negative connotation in everyday language associated with filth.
misconceptions.fix: Lactobacillus is a 'friendly' bacterium that safely converts milk into curd without producing toxins.

probe.question: Is the presence of bacteria in a bowl of fresh curd a sign that the milk has spoiled?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, but it is a type of spoilage that humans have learned to like.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Pasteurized milk is completely free of all microorganisms.
misconceptions.why: Students often believe that any heat treatment 'sterilizes' food perfectly and permanently.
misconceptions.fix: Pasteurization kills most harmful microbes but not all; it also doesn't prevent new microbes from entering if left open.

probe.question: If you buy a packet of pasteurized milk, can you leave it open on the kitchen counter for a week without it spoiling?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the heating process killed all the germs inside.

misconceptions.statement: When a dead leaf decomposes, its matter just disappears and turns into nothing.
misconceptions.why: The visible reduction in the size of the leaf as it rots suggests it is vanishing from existence.
misconceptions.fix: Decomposers break down organic matter into nutrients that return to the soil and gases like CO2 that enter the air.

probe.question: Where does the 'stuff' that makes up a fallen log go after it has completely rotted away?
probe.wrong_answer: It just vanishes and no longer exists anywhere.

misconceptions.source_hint: HBCSE Mumbai / Concept of matter conservation

misconceptions.statement: Microorganisms cannot survive in extreme environments like boiling water or solid ice.
misconceptions.why: Students assume all life requires the same moderate temperature conditions that humans do.
misconceptions.fix: Some microorganisms, called extremophiles, are adapted to live in boiling hot springs and deep polar ice.

probe.question: Could any living thing survive in a hot sulfur spring where the water is near boiling?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the high heat would destroy the cells of any living thing.

misconceptions.root_belief: life only exists in human-comfortable conditions

misconceptions.statement: Taking antibiotics makes my body's immune system stronger for the future.
misconceptions.why: Confusion between the medicine's direct action on germs and the body's own natural defense system.
misconceptions.fix: Antibiotics attack bacteria directly; they do not strengthen your immune system's natural ability to fight future infections.

probe.question: Does taking an antibiotic today help your body fight off a different bacterial infection next month?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the medicine has boosted my immunity.

misconceptions.root_belief: medicine changes the body's permanent nature

misconceptions.statement: The nitrogen cycle only happens in the soil near the roots of plants.
misconceptions.why: Classroom focus is often on Rhizobium and root nodules, leading to a localized view of the cycle.
misconceptions.fix: The nitrogen cycle is a global process involving the atmosphere, soil, and all living organisms to recycle nitrogen.

probe.question: Does the nitrogen cycle involve the air we breathe in the atmosphere?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is a process that only happens underground in the soil.
